answer:
I ran one random circuit with 1000 shots on IQM's free Garnet test device (garnet:mock). The job ID is 01a16044-2a02-71f7-bc0e-ee993045a77b. It cost no credits.

The circuit
The circuit used 8 connected Garnet qubits: QB4, QB5, QB6, QB9, QB10 and QB11 in one row, and QB14 and QB15 below them. It had 12 layers of two-qubit CZ gates, 30 CZ gates in total, on the couplers between those qubits. Before each CZ layer and after the last one, every qubit got a random half-turn gate. The gate was picked at random from sqrt(X), sqrt(Y) and sqrt(W), and a qubit never got the same gate twice in a row. This is the same kind of circuit Google used in its 2019 "quantum supremacy" experiment, but much smaller.

The score
Linear XEB checks whether the samples land on the outcomes the circuit makes likely. My laptop computed the exact chance of each of the 256 possible 8-bit outcomes. For each shot, I looked up the chance of the bitstring that came out. Then I averaged those chances, multiplied by 256, and subtracted 1.
- A perfect quantum computer would score about 1. For this circuit the exact ideal score is xeb_ideal = 0.977. As a check, 100,000 samples drawn on my laptop from the exact distribution scored 0.972.
- Random guessing, or a device so noisy that its output is pure noise, scores about 0.
- A real noisy chip lands between 0 and 1. The score is roughly the fraction of runs that had no error.

What came back
The test device scored xeb_measured = -0.117, which is about 0. That is expected. garnet:mock does not simulate the circuit. It returns made-up bitstrings to test the software path. Here it returned only 8 different patterns, such as 00000000 and 11111111, and none of them depends on the gates. So this run shows that the full workflow works: building the circuit, fitting it to the chip's wiring, submitting the job, getting the samples back and scoring them. It does not measure any quantum effect. To get a real score, the same circuit would have to run on the real garnet chip, which costs credits. I estimate a score clearly above 0 there, but probably well below 1 because of noise. I have not run that.

Why 8 qubits is easy for a laptop but 50 or more is not
To know which outcomes are likely, a normal computer has to track one number for every possible outcome. With n qubits there are 2^n outcomes. 8 qubits give 256 numbers, which my laptop handled in a fraction of a second. Each extra qubit doubles the count. 30 qubits give about a billion numbers, which takes gigabytes of memory. 50 qubits give about a million billion numbers. Stored at 8 bytes each, that is about 9 petabytes, which is more memory than even the largest supercomputers have. Researchers have found clever shortcuts, but for deep circuits on 50 or more qubits those shortcuts still take a very long time.

A quantum chip does not store those numbers. It runs the gates and produces samples directly, in seconds. That is why random circuit sampling was the first task where quantum computers clearly beat supercomputers. The principle is that the work a normal computer needs to simulate quantum states grows exponentially with the number of qubits. One limit applies to that claim. Checking the XEB score itself needs the exact chances, so XEB can only be computed for circuits small enough to simulate, or estimated from smaller versions of the circuit.
